definition: One processor execution unit that runs an instruction stream. A single-core MCU runs one such stream at a time, while peripherals such as DMA can operate concurrently; multiple cores can execute separate threads simultaneously.
example: The Raspberry Pi 5 has four Cortex-A76 cores; the Daisy Seed's STM32H750 has one Cortex-M7 core.

definition: Arm's family of 32-bit processor cores for microcontrollers. The Cortex-M7 implementations on Daisy Seed and Teensy 4.x include hardware floating-point support; optional core features and debug facilities depend on the exact implementation.
example: The Daisy Seed's Cortex-M7 runs at 480 MHz; the Teensy 4.1's at 600 MHz.

definition: Arm's family of application processor cores, designed to run full operating systems such as Linux, with features like virtual memory that Cortex-M cores lack. The Raspberry Pi 5 uses four Cortex-A76 cores.
example: The Raspberry Pi 5's quad-core Cortex-A76 runs at 2.4 GHz.

definition: The version of Arm's architecture (the rules for instructions, registers and debug features) that Cortex-M3, M4 and M7 cores implement. It defines the optional DWT cycle counter and exclusive load/store instructions for 8-, 16- and 32-bit values, but none for 64-bit values.

The standard way computers store signed (positive and negative) integers. The top bit acts as the sign, so a 16-bit value runs from −32,768 to +32,767. Audio codecs send samples in two's complement, most significant bit first.
example: In 16-bit two's complement, 0xFFFF means −1 and 0x8000 means −32,768.

definition: The bit that says whether a signed number is negative. In two's complement it is the most significant bit (MSB): 1 means negative.
example: If a receiver misreads an I2S word by one bit, it takes the wrong bit as the sign and samples flip between positive and negative.

definition: A decimal unit of data size equal to one billion bytes; hardware documentation sometimes uses memory-size labels inconsistently. Check whether a source means decimal GB or binary GiB instead of inferring capacity from the label alone.
example: The Pi 5 product brief lists RAM configurations in GB.

definition: Most significant bit: the bit worth the most in a binary number (the leftmost when written down). Sending MSB first means the highest-value bit goes out on the wire first, as in I2S audio.
example: In 0111 1111, the MSB is the leading 0.

definition: Writing numbers in base 16, with the digits 0–9 and A–F, usually marked with a 0x prefix. Each hex digit stands for exactly 4 bits, which makes bit patterns easy to read.
example: 0x7F is 0111 1111 in binary: 127.

definition: Writing numbers in base 2, using only the digits 0 and 1, which is how digital hardware stores every value. Each position is worth twice the one to its right.
example: Three select lines can show the binary patterns 000 to 111: eight combinations.

definition: Non-volatile memory that keeps its contents with the power off. On a microcontroller it stores the program and constant data; SSDs and SD cards are built from it too. It is fast to read but slow to erase and rewrite, and writing firmware into it is called 'flashing'.
example: The Daisy Seed has 128 KB of internal flash plus an 8 MB external QSPI flash chip.

definition: Writing a firmware image into a board's flash memory, either over USB through a bootloader or through a debug probe. After flashing and a reset, the board runs the new program.
example: `make program-dfu` flashes a Daisy Seed over USB DFU.

definition: Memory that keeps its contents when the power is removed, such as flash, ROM and EEPROM. Your firmware lives in it.
example: Unplug a flashed board for a year and the program is still there, because flash is non-volatile.

definition: Memory that loses its contents when the power is removed, such as RAM. It holds variables, the stack and audio buffers while the program runs. (Not to be confused with C's volatile keyword.)
Static RAM: fast memory that keeps data as long as power is on, without the refreshing DRAM needs. A microcontroller's main working memory is on-chip SRAM.
example: The Daisy bootloader can run programs of up to roughly 480 KB from the Seed's SRAM at near internal-flash speed.

definition: Data tightly coupled memory: RAM connected through a dedicated processor interface rather than the ordinary cache path. It can provide predictable low-latency CPU access, but DMA accessibility and placement rules are target-specific.
example: The Daisy build memory map lists 128 KB of DTCM; do not assume a DMA peripheral can use every CPU-accessible region.

definition: Synchronous dynamic RAM: dense, cheap memory on a separate chip. It is slower to access than on-chip SRAM, so it suits large data such as long delay lines and samples rather than hot code.
example: The Daisy Seed has a 64 MB SDRAM chip.

definition: Pseudo-static RAM: a dynamic RAM chip with its own refresh logic, so it can be used almost like simple static RAM. Teensy 4.1 has pads on the underside for adding PSRAM chips for several extra megabytes.

Quad SPI: a serial-memory interface using four data lines during supported transfer phases, increasing data throughput relative to a one-line phase. Execution speed depends on clocks, caches, placement and workload; the Daisy bootloader guide describes its QSPI-hosted programs as slower than its SRAM-hosted programs.
example: The Daisy Seed's 8 MB program flash is a QSPI chip; the libDaisy guide says BOOT_QSPI programs run 'a fair bit slower'.

definition: Read-only memory: storage intended to be read rather than rewritten during ordinary operation. Factory system bootloaders can reside in mask ROM that application flash programming cannot erase.
example: The STM32H750 system bootloader resides separately from application flash; access still depends on the documented boot and protection configuration.

definition: Electrically erasable programmable read-only memory: a small non-volatile memory that can be rewritten a byte at a time. Raspberry Pi HATs carry one that identifies the board so Linux can configure it automatically.

A small, fast storage location within a processor core, used directly by instructions for operands, addresses or state. These registers are volatile working storage, distinct from the persistent firmware image.
example: A compiler may keep a variable in a register inside a loop, which is why a plain variable can miss another side's update.

definition: A memory address inside a peripheral or external chip that configures or reports on the hardware. Writing to it changes what the hardware does, for example powering up a codec's DAC or setting a timer's rate.
example: To make a control-port codec produce sound, firmware writes a sequence of registers over I2C: power, format, routing, volume, unmute.

definition: A dedicated hardware block on a microcontroller that does one job without the CPU's constant attention, such as a timer, ADC, UART, I2C, SPI, SAI or DMA controller. Peripherals let the CPU spend its time on DSP.
example: The SAI peripheral clocks samples out to the codec while the CPU computes the next block.

definition: A peripheral that counts clock ticks and can trigger an interrupt, an ADC reading or a pin change at a precise, steady rate, independently of the code that is running.
example: A timer firing every 1 ms can be used to poll buttons and scan knobs.

definition: Software closely tied to a device and its hardware, commonly stored in non-volatile memory. Bare-metal MCU firmware normally starts through reset/start-up code and keeps running; firmware can also use an RTOS.
example: Your synth's firmware sets up the codec, starts the audio callback and then loops forever reading controls.

definition: Running directly on hardware without an operating system. Timing and startup depend on the firmware, interrupt design, peripherals and boot path; removing an OS does not itself prove deadlines or instant readiness.
example: A Daisy Seed running libDaisy is a bare-metal system.

definition: Real-time operating system: an OS designed to support priority-based tasks and timing requirements. A system meets its deadlines only when task priorities, execution times, blocking and hardware behavior are correctly designed and analysed.
example: On an RTOS, a high-priority audio task blocked on a lock held by a low-priority task suffers priority inversion.

definition: The software that manages a computer's hardware and runs programs on top of it, handling memory, files, devices and scheduling. A Raspberry Pi runs one (Linux); a bare-metal microcontroller does not.
example: A desktop OS can terminate a failed application; bare-metal firmware needs its own fault handling or watchdog recovery.

definition: The part of an operating system that selects runnable tasks or threads for CPU execution. Priorities, scheduling policy and other system work affect audio timing; having or omitting an OS alone does not prove deadline reliability.

A timer that can raise a fault or reset action if firmware does not service it as specified. In the described MCU design it can restart hung firmware; the exact timeout, reset scope and recovery behavior depend on configuration.
example: If only the main loop services a watchdog configured for a 500 ms timeout, a long enough main-loop freeze can trigger its configured reset action.

definition: A button or signal that invokes a documented processor/system reset path. Reset is not necessarily identical to removing power: retained memory and peripheral reset scope depend on the hardware. On Daisy Seed, holding BOOT while pressing RESET selects the ROM bootloader.

A button on the Daisy Seed that selects what runs after reset. Held while RESET is pressed, it starts the STM32's factory ROM bootloader for DFU flashing; it can also extend the Daisy bootloader's grace period.
The small piece of code that runs first after reset: it sets up the stack, copies initial values into RAM, configures clocks and then calls main. What happens if main returns depends on it.
The interval from power-on or reset until a specified state is ready, such as audio output. Bootloaders, peripheral initialisation and the application affect it; measure the complete configuration.
example: An application with a 2.5-second bootloader grace period is not instantly ready.

definition: A program that prepares or launches application firmware, often also providing an update path. Whether it runs at every power-up, supports USB programming or is protected from application writes depends on the platform.
example: STM32 system recovery can use ROM code; Teensy has a separate programming chip, while its ordinary application can start directly.

definition: A loader supplied in a chip’s read-only memory. On supported STM32 parts and configurations it provides recovery independently of broken application flash; hardware failure, protection settings and unavailable interfaces can still prevent recovery.
example: On the Daisy Seed, hold BOOT and press RESET to start the ST system bootloader.

definition: An optional second-stage bootloader from Electro-Smith that sits in the Daisy Seed's internal flash and loads larger programs into SRAM or the external QSPI flash. After reset it waits a 2.5-second grace period for DFU or a binary on SD card or USB drive.

A separate processor on Teensy 4.x that controls programming of the main processor. Ordinary application flashing cannot overwrite that loader, providing a recovery route independent of the application; hardware and security conditions still apply.
Device Firmware Upgrade: a standard USB device class for updating firmware. A board in DFU mode appears on the computer as a DFU device, and a tool such as dfu-util writes the new image.
example: The Daisy Seed's ROM bootloader enumerates as a USB DFU device.

definition: A free command-line program that writes firmware to devices in USB DFU mode. The Daisy toolchain's `make program-dfu` uses it.
Electro-Smith's browser-based tool that flashes a Daisy over USB DFU without installing a toolchain.
PJRC's application that flashes .hex files to a Teensy over USB through its bootloader chip. The Arduino IDE (with Teensyduino) starts it automatically after compiling.

The pushbutton on a Teensy that puts it into programming mode through the bootloader chip. It is not a reset button. PJRC states that holding it for 13–17 seconds erases the flash and restores a simple LED-blink program.
example: PJRC documents a 13–17-second erase/restore. Its loader page says the blink restore copy is created on a prior normal short press.

definition: Describes a device that no longer works or accepts new firmware, as useless as a brick. A protected bootloader means a 'bricked' microcontroller board can almost always be recovered.

A PJRC feature that locks a Teensy 4.x so only encrypted firmware can be loaded. PJRC notes that in secure mode JTAG can no longer access the chip's internal memory, so the normal bootloader route is replaced by a small loader utility.
A small hardware adapter that connects a computer to a microcontroller's debug port (SWD or JTAG). Through it a debugger can flash firmware, stop the CPU, set breakpoints and inspect memory.
example: Electro-Smith recommends the ST-Link V3 Mini probe for the Daisy Seed.

definition: Serial Wire Debug: Arm's debug-access interface using a clock and bidirectional data signal, with an appropriate ground reference. It provides processor debug access with fewer signal pins than JTAG, but does not replace JTAG boundary-scan testing.

The IEEE 1149.1 test-access interface, named after the Joint Test Action Group, commonly using four main signals plus optional reset. Chips may also expose processor debugging through it; supported ports depend on the chip and board.
STMicroelectronics' debug probe for its STM32 chips, which connects over SWD or JTAG. The V3 Mini is a small, cheap version that Electro-Smith recommends for debugging the Daisy Seed.
Open On-Chip Debugger: free software that drives a debug probe, flashing chips and acting as a server that GDB connects to.
The GNU Project's debugger. Connected to a microcontroller through a probe and OpenOCD, it can halt the CPU, set breakpoints, step through code and read variables.
A program that lets you stop a running program, step through it line by line and inspect its variables and memory. On a microcontroller it works through a debug probe.
A marker that makes the debugger halt the CPU when execution reaches a chosen line. Halting inside the audio callback stops new samples being computed, so the codec may buzz on stale buffers.
Running a halted program one statement or instruction at a time under a debugger, to watch exactly what it does.

A Cortex-M fault exception used for certain serious errors and faults escalated from other handlers. Its cause and saved exception state can help locate the failure, although not every fault supplies an exact address for the offending instruction.
Compiling on one kind of computer for a different kind of CPU: the compiler runs on your laptop but produces machine code for the microcontroller.
example: Building Daisy firmware on a Mac with the GNU Arm toolchain is cross-compiling for a Cortex-M7.

definition: Compiling code for the same kind of CPU the compiler runs on, as you do for an ordinary desktop program.
The binary instructions a particular CPU executes directly. A compiler turns source code into machine code for its target CPU.
The set of programs that turn source code into a firmware image: compiler, assembler, linker and related tools. Cortex-M boards normally use the GNU Arm toolchain (arm-none-eabi-gcc).
A free-software project whose tools, including the GCC compiler and the GDB debugger, form the standard open-source toolchain for Arm microcontrollers.
The build tool that combines compiled pieces of code into one program and decides where each part goes in memory. It reports an error if the program does not fit a memory region.
example: A 150 KB program fails to link for the Daisy Seed's 128 KB internal flash.

definition: A file that tells the linker which memory regions a chip has and which parts of the program go in each, such as code in flash and buffers in SRAM or SDRAM. On embedded targets it strongly affects speed.
example: libDaisy's linker script is named after the STM32H750IB.

definition: A text file format for firmware images: each line is a record giving an address and some bytes, written in hexadecimal. The Teensy Loader flashes .hex files.

Executable and Linkable Format: a format for object files and program images used by the GNU embedded toolchain. An ELF can include debug symbols when built with them; stripped or non-debug images need not contain those symbols.
Extra information in a build that links machine-code addresses back to source files, lines and variable names, so a debugger can show where you are in your code.

A value a process reports to its hosting environment when it exits, commonly zero for success. A bare-metal firmware main function has no desktop operating system receiving an exit status; its runtime determines what returning does.

A compiler setting (such as -O0 for debugging or -O2 for speed) that controls how aggressively it rearranges and shortens code. The same source can run at very different speeds in a debug build and an optimised one.
A plain, programming-like description of an algorithm that is not tied to any real language's rules, used to show the idea rather than runnable code.
The 64-bit instruction set used by most Intel and AMD desktop and laptop CPUs. Code compiled for it cannot run on an Arm microcontroller, hence cross-compiling.
Apple's own Arm-based processors (M1 and later) used in Macs since 2020. They are Arm, but application processors, not Cortex-M, so firmware is still cross-compiled.
Integrated development environment: an editor that also builds, uploads and debugs code from one window, such as the Arduino IDE or VS Code.
Microsoft's free code editor. With extensions it builds, flashes and debugs microcontroller firmware; Electro-Smith's Daisy guide uses it.
An open-source electronics platform with a beginner-friendly IDE and C++ library for programming microcontroller boards. Teensy and Daisy can both be programmed through it.
PJRC's add-on that lets the Arduino IDE build and upload programs for Teensy boards, including the Teensy Audio Library.
A cross-platform build system and editor plug-in for embedded development that supports Teensy, STM32 and many other boards.
A file of build rules read by the make tool. The Daisy examples use one, so `make` builds the firmware and `make program-dfu` flashes it.

General-purpose input/output: a microcontroller pin that firmware can set as a digital input (reading 0 or 1) or a digital output (driving 0 V or the supply voltage). Buttons, switches and LEDs connect to GPIO pins.
example: The Daisy Seed has 31 GPIO pins.

definition: The voltage ranges a digital circuit treats as 0 (low, near 0 V) and 1 (high, near the supply). Voltages in between are undefined, so a pin may read either.
example: On a 3.3 V microcontroller, a voltage near 3.3 V reads as logic 1.

definition: A pin configured to read a voltage as a logic 0 or 1. It draws almost no current, so if nothing drives it, it floats.

A pin configured to drive a logic-low or logic-high voltage while sourcing or sinking a limited current. Real output voltages depend on loading and the datasheet guarantees; they are not necessarily exactly ground or supply.
example: PJRC recommends no more than 4 mA from each Teensy 4.1 output pin.

definition: The Arduino-style pin mode that makes a pin a digital input with its internal pull-up resistor switched on, ready for an active-low button wired to ground.
example: On Teensy 4.x, INPUT_PULLUP selects the pad's 22 kΩ pull-up setting.

definition: An input rating allowing a specified 5 V signal under documented supply, pin and operating-mode conditions. It is not permission to apply 5 V in an unsupported analogue mode or while unpowered; check the exact pin limits.
example: Teensy 4.1 pins are not 5 V tolerant; most Daisy Seed Rev 7 pins are.

definition: A circuit or chip that converts a digital signal from one logic voltage to another, for example from 5 V to 3.3 V, so parts with different supplies can talk safely.
An output pin sources current when it drives high and pushes current out into a load, and sinks current when it drives low and lets current flow in from a load to ground. Both have datasheet limits.
The most current a microcontroller pin, or the whole chip, may source or sink. Exceeding the per-pin or total limit can damage the chip or disturb its supply.
example: Sixteen LEDs at 4 mA is 64 mA, which may exceed a chip's total limit even if each pin is fine.

definition: An input pin connected to nothing. Because it has very high impedance, stray charge and noise decide its voltage, so it reads random 0s and 1s. A pull resistor fixes it.
Offering a large opposition to current, so almost no current flows. A digital input is high impedance, which is why it floats when left unconnected.
The total opposition a circuit offers to an alternating current, measured in ohms. Output impedance says how stiffly a source drives; input impedance how much a load draws.
example: The Daisy Seed's audio output impedance is 100 Ω; a line input is typically around 10 kΩ or more.

definition: A resistor that gives a digital input a default level when nothing else drives it: a pull-up to the supply makes it read 1, a pull-down to ground makes it read 0.

A resistor from a signal line to the supply voltage, so the line reads 1 unless something pulls it low. Buttons to ground and I2C buses both rely on them; internal pull-ups are typically tens of kilohms.
example: A 10 kΩ pull-up to 3.3 V passes about 0.33 mA while its button is held, assuming the switch has negligible resistance.

definition: A resistor from a signal line to ground, so the line reads 0 unless something drives it high.
example: A button wired to 3.3 V needs a pull-down so the pin reads 0 when released.

definition: A signal whose 'on' or 'asserted' state is the low voltage (0). A button wired to ground with a pull-up is active-low: pressed reads 0. SPI chip-select lines are active-low too.

A chosen voltage reference and current-return network for a circuit; it need not be connected to protective earth. Direct non-isolated single-ended logic usually needs a suitable shared reference, while an isolated interface such as DIN MIDI deliberately avoids a galvanic signal-ground connection.
An unwanted current path created when equipment is connected to ground in more than one place, which often causes hum and noise. MIDI's opto-isolated input exists to avoid them.
The rapid on-off chatter of mechanical switch contacts for a short time after they close or open. A microcontroller sees one press as a burst of transitions unless it debounces.
example: Jack Ganssle tested 18 switches: excluding two outliers (one pushbutton bounced for 157 ms on release), the other 16 averaged about 1.6 ms of bounce.

definition: Filtering out switch bounce so one press gives exactly one press event, in software (by sampling the switch over time) or in hardware (an RC filter plus a Schmitt trigger). In software generally, debouncing also means waiting for a burst of events to settle before acting.
example: A 20 ms debounce period is a conservative starting point.

definition: A debouncing method that accepts the first change immediately and then ignores the pin for a fixed time. It responds fastest but treats a single noise spike as a press.
A debouncing method that accepts a new state only after the input has disagreed with the current state for N consecutive readings; any bounce back resets the count.
example: With one reading per millisecond and a five-reading threshold, acceptance occurs on the fifth agreeing reading; delay from a physical edge also depends on its position between samples.

definition: A store of bits that moves along one place each time a new bit is pushed in. In software it debounces (wait for a pattern such as 0111 1111); as a chip it turns a few serial pins into many LED outputs.
example: libDaisy's Switch class reports a press when its 8-bit shift register reads 0x7F.

definition: A debouncing method that keeps a counter between 0 and a top value: add one for each pressed reading, subtract one for each released reading. Its state changes only at the ends, so occasional wrong readings slow it down without resetting it.
PJRC's (and the Arduino community's) library for reading pushbuttons with debouncing, using a time interval in milliseconds.
Checking an input repeatedly at regular intervals, rather than having it raise an interrupt. Buttons are best polled on a steady tick, around every 1 ms.
One regular, timer-driven step of a periodic task, for example every 1 ms. Debouncers and knob scanners usually run once per tick.
Waiting by running a loop that does nothing useful until time passes or a condition becomes true. Inside an interrupt it blocks everything at that priority or lower.
example: A 20 ms busy-wait in a button interrupt could miss 20 audio blocks of 1 ms.

definition: Light-emitting diode: a semiconductor that glows when current flows through it in one direction. Its current must be limited, normally with a series resistor.
example: A red indicator LED is often bright enough at 1–2 mA.

definition: The voltage across a diode or LED while forward current flows. It depends on current, temperature and the selected part; use specified minimum/maximum limits at the intended conditions for design, rather than treating it as an exact fixed drop.
example: A nominal 2.0 V LED at the chosen current leaves nominally 1.3 V for a resistor from 3.3 V.

definition: A resistor in the same branch as a component, so the same branch current flows through both. A suitable value can limit current; safety still depends on supply, component behavior, tolerance and ratings.
example: With an assumed 3.3 V source and 2.0 V LED drop, 330 Ω gives a nominal current of about 3.9 mA; this is not a worst-case rating check.

definition: A chip that switches and limits current for many LEDs, controlled from the microcontroller by a few serial pins. It saves pins and keeps LED current off the microcontroller.
A chip that adds extra digital input or output pins to a microcontroller, controlled over I2C or SPI.
Pulse-width modulation: switching an output fully on and off rapidly and varying the fraction of time it is on. It dims LEDs and, with filtering, makes analogue voltages.
example: An LED driven with 25% PWM is on a quarter of the time, so it gives out about a quarter of the light.

definition: A semiconductor switch or amplifier: a small current or voltage at one terminal controls a larger current through the other two. A microcontroller pin can switch a transistor that powers many LEDs.
How far a component's real value may differ from its marked value, as a percentage. A 330 Ω 5% resistor may be anywhere from about 314 Ω to 347 Ω.

Preferred component-value series arranged approximately logarithmically within each decade. A calculated nominal lower resistance bound of 325 ohms suggests 330 ohms in E12, but current limits still require tolerance, supply and LED-voltage checks.
An input with built-in hysteresis: it switches high at one voltage and low at a lower one, so a slowly changing or noisy signal gives one clean transition.
A simple filter made of a resistor (R) and a capacitor (C). As a low-pass filter it smooths fast changes, such as switch bounce, before a Schmitt-trigger input.
example: 1 kΩ with 100 nF gives a cut-off frequency of about 1.6 kHz.

definition: A two-terminal component made to have a specified resistance, measured in ohms. Within its power and voltage ratings an ordinary resistor is close to ohmic: the current through it is proportional to the voltage across it (Ohm's law). Its real value differs from the marking by its tolerance and drifts slightly with temperature.
example: A 10 kΩ pull-up with 3.3 V across it passes about 0.33 mA.

definition: A component that stores charge with a voltage difference between its terminals. An ideal capacitor carries current when that voltage changes and blocks steady DC current after settling; a real part has leakage and voltage/polarity limits. It can still hold a steady voltage.
Complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor: the transistor technology used in almost all modern digital chips. CMOS inputs draw almost no current, which is why they float when unconnected.
example: The CD4051 multiplexer is a CMOS part.

definition: A tiny unwanted current that flows through an insulator or a switched-off transistor. On a floating input, leakage and stray fields decide the voltage.

For an ohmic component, such as an ordinary resistor within its ratings, the voltage across it equals the current through it times its resistance (V = I × R), so current is proportional to voltage. Many parts are not ohmic: an LED's or diode's current rises steeply and non-linearly with voltage. In an LED circuit, apply Ohm's law to the series resistor, not to the LED.
example: 3.3 V across 10 kΩ drives about 0.33 mA; the same voltage across 1 kΩ drives about ten times as much.

definition: A component whose current is directly proportional to the voltage across it, so its resistance stays constant and Ohm's law applies. Ordinary resistors are close to ohmic within their ratings. LEDs and other diodes are non-ohmic: their current rises steeply and non-linearly over a narrow range of voltage, and the forward voltage at a given current varies with temperature, colour and the particular part rather than being a fixed threshold.
example: Doubling the voltage across a 10 kΩ resistor doubles its current; a few tenths of a volt more across an LED can multiply its current many times.

definition: One thousandth of a volt (symbol mV).
example: One 12-bit ADC step over 3.3 V is about 0.81 mV.

definition: One millionth of a volt (symbol µV).
example: An ideal 16-bit converter spanning 3.3 V has a code spacing of about 50 µV; useful resolution also depends on actual noise and errors.

definition: The SI unit of electric current (symbol A): how much charge flows past a point per second.
One thousandth of an ampere (symbol mA). Microcontroller pins and LEDs work in single milliamperes.
example: PJRC recommends at most 4 mA per Teensy 4.1 output.

definition: The SI unit of resistance and impedance (symbol Ω).
One thousand ohms (symbol kΩ).
example: A typical external pull-up is 4.7–10 kΩ.

definition: One thousand million hertz (symbol GHz), used for desktop and Raspberry Pi processor clocks.

How many clock cycles occur per second. Instruction throughput, memory waits, peripherals and implementation affect how much useful work fits within those cycles; clock-rate ratios alone do not predict synth voice counts.
example: 600 MHz versus 480 MHz is a ratio of clocks, not of synth voices.

definition: A reusable plastic board with rows of spring contacts for building circuits without soldering.
A short wire with pins or sockets on each end, used to connect points on a breadboard or between boards. Long jumpers are a poor choice for fast clock signals.
A small circuit board that carries one chip and brings its pins out to easy-to-wire headers, often with the supporting parts the chip needs.
A row of metal pins on a board for connecting wires or other boards.
example: The Raspberry Pi 5 has a 40-pin GPIO header.

definition: Printed circuit board: a board with copper tracks that connect the components soldered to it. Its layout affects how much digital noise reaches the audio.
Joining components and wires with melted metal (solder) to make permanent electrical connections.
A numbered version of a circuit board. Revisions can change major parts, so a fact true for one revision may be false for another.
example: The Daisy Seed has used three codecs: AK4556 (Rev 4), WM8731 (Rev 5) and PCM3060 (Rev 7).

definition: Having matching pin positions and intended signal functions. Replacement still needs voltage, timing, power and software compatibility checks; matching pin locations alone does not establish complete interchangeability.
example: Daisy Seed revisions 5 and 7 are pin compatible.

definition: A pin that a board ties to ground to identify its revision, so software can detect which hardware it is running on.
example: Rev 5 Daisy Seeds ground PD3; Rev 7 ground PD5.

definition: An instrument that draws voltage against time, so you can see signals such as clock edges or a GPIO pulse marking how long the audio callback runs.

An instrument that samples digital logic levels against time, often on several channels, and may decode buses such as I2C, SPI and UART. Timing resolution, voltage limits and channel bandwidth must suit the measurement.
How long a pulse stays high. With a GPIO set high during the callback, the pulse width is the callback's run time.
Unwanted oscillation after a sharp signal edge, caused by the inductance and capacitance of wires. On long wires it can create false clock edges.
Unwanted leakage of one signal into another. With a multiplexer, reading too soon after switching makes one knob's value bleed into the next.
How faithfully a digital signal keeps its intended shape and timing as it travels along wires. Long wires and poor grounds degrade it.
A short spike in the current a circuit draws, for example when the CPU switches from heavy work to idle. Through shared ground it can leak into audio as a tone.
Small unwanted variations riding on a power-supply voltage. They add noise to ADC readings and audio.
The household AC supply (230 V at 50 Hz in the UK). This course keeps to low-voltage battery or USB power; mains wiring is dangerous.
example: Mains hum in the UK is at 50 Hz and its harmonics.

definition: The input-voltage pin on a development board, which feeds the board's own regulators.
example: The Daisy Seed accepts 5–17 V on VIN.

definition: The number of bits in each converter reading, which sets how many distinct codes there are (2 to the power of the bits). Noise limits how many of those bits are meaningful.
example: PJRC says Teensy 4.1's ADC allows 12 bits, but only about 10 are normally usable due to noise.

definition: The voltage an ADC treats as full scale: inputs at (or just below) it give the highest code. One step is the reference voltage divided by the number of codes.
example: Daisy Seed and Teensy 4.1 analogue inputs both run from 0 to 3.3 V.

definition: A variable resistor with a sliding contact (the wiper). Wired across a supply it forms an adjustable voltage divider, which is how a synth knob makes a voltage for an ADC.
example: The Daisy Seed datasheet's example knob is a 10 kΩ linear pot.

definition: The sliding contact of a potentiometer, whose voltage moves between the two ends as you turn the knob.
How a potentiometer's resistance changes with rotation: linear, or audio/logarithmic for volume. With an ADC it is usually easier to use a linear pot and apply the curve in software.

A series network with output measured at a junction relative to a reference node. For two resistors with negligible loading, the ratio is set by their resistances; connecting a load changes that ratio.
A separately filtered supply for analogue parts such as ADCs and pots, kept quieter than the digital supply.
example: Daisy's ADC guide wires the pot's top end to 3v3_A.

definition: A tiny capacitor inside an ADC that is charged to the input voltage and then measured. The source must charge it quickly, which is why very high-value pots and fast multiplexer switching cause errors.

Time after a change until a signal enters and remains within a specified error band around its final value. Multiplexed ADC acquisition must allow the required settling and sampling time; exact mathematical equality is not the practical criterion.

A switch chip that connects one of several inputs to a single output, chosen by digital select lines. An analogue multiplexer passes analogue voltages in either direction, so one ADC pin can read many knobs in turn.
example: One CD4051 connects any of 8 knobs to one ADC pin using 3 select lines.

definition: A common, inexpensive CMOS 8-channel analogue multiplexer: three select inputs choose which of eight pins connects to the common pin.
A digital control input that chooses which channel a multiplexer connects. Each extra line doubles the number of channels.
How many times per second every knob in a multiplexed set is read.
example: Eight knobs on one mux at a 1 kHz scan rate need 8,000 ADC conversions a second.

definition: Unwanted small variation in something that should be steady: in a reading (a still knob's ADC value wandering by a few codes) or in timing (when a callback starts or how long it runs). (In retry back-off, 'jitter' instead means randomness added on purpose.)
Constant spurious change events from a control that is not moving, caused by noise in its readings, such as a flood of MIDI CC messages from an untouched knob.

A filter that outputs the average of a recent window of readings. Averaging uncorrelated zero-mean noise reduces its variance; correlated noise can remain. A full fixed window has a delay of half one less than its length, measured in reading intervals, away from response zeros.

A filter with one pole and one feedback-state value. A first-order low-pass smoother with a coefficient above zero and no greater than one moves that fraction of the remaining gap toward each input, without overshooting a fixed target. Its time constant in seconds depends on the coefficient and the update rate; other one-pole designs and coefficient ranges behave differently.
example: With a coefficient of about 0.095 at 1,000 readings a second, it covers 63% of a step in 10 ms.

definition: The characteristic time of a first-order (one-pole) exponential response. After one time constant a step response has covered about 63.2% of the change, after about three about 95%, and in exact arithmetic it never quite arrives. A discrete smoother's time constant depends on both its coefficient and its update rate; a library's differently defined slew or ramp time need not equal it.
example: A 10 ms time constant at 1,000 readings a second uses a per-reading fraction of about 0.095.

definition: Making a system's response depend on its recent state, here by holding a value until the input moves further than a threshold. It stops a still knob producing constant tiny changes.
example: With a ±3-code band, ADC readings jittering between 2046 and 2050 hold at 2048.

definition: A mapping in which equal steps of the input give equal steps of the output. For a knob it converts the 0–1 control value to a parameter range evenly, which suits pan position or a mix ratio.

A mapping for which equal input increments give equal positive output ratios. It spreads a wide frequency, time or gain range across a control; equal perceived changes are not guaranteed for every sound or parameter.
example: Mapping 20 Hz–20 kHz exponentially puts 632 Hz at the knob's centre.

definition: The mathematical constant e, about 2.71828, the base of natural exponential growth and decay. The exponential time-constant rule for choosing a one-pole smoother's coefficient uses it.

For non-negative integer exponents, one or repeated products of two: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on. A power-of-two ring capacity permits slot wrapping with a bit mask; the counter-width and occupancy invariants still need checking.
The rule for how a mixer sets the left and right gains as a sound is panned, chosen so its loudness stays roughly even across the stereo field.

Reassigning an occupied synthesis voice to a new note when no free voice is available. The selection and transition must stay within the callback budget, and abrupt replacement can click; it need not be an unbounded or slow operation.
A stored set of parameter values recalled together to change the sound. Loading one should update every parameter at once.
The slower rate at which control values such as knobs are read and processed, often around 1 kHz, compared with the audio sample rate.
Running at the audio sample rate, once per sample, as opposed to once per block or at control rate.
A Texas Instruments 24-bit stereo audio codec (ADC up to 96 kHz, DAC up to 192 kHz). The Daisy Seed Rev 7 uses it in hardware mode, set by pin levels rather than I2C, with 24-bit left-justified data.
example: Its DAC digital filter has a group delay of 20 sample periods.

definition: A low-power stereo audio codec from Wolfson (now Cirrus Logic), configured over I2C. The Daisy Seed Rev 5 used it.
An Asahi Kasei (AKM) 24-bit stereo audio codec, used on the Daisy Seed Rev 4.
An NXP low-power stereo audio codec with a headphone amplifier, controlled over I2C. It is the converter on PJRC's Teensy audio adaptor, running at 16-bit 44.1 kHz with the Teensy Audio Library.
A Texas Instruments stereo audio DAC chip (output only), used on the Raspberry Pi DAC+, which Raspberry Pi describes as 24-bit 192 kHz.
A codec configuration method where settings such as the data format are fixed by tying pins high or low on the board, so no I2C register writes are needed.
example: The Daisy Seed Rev 7's PCM3060 runs in hardware mode.

definition: A digital interface through which firmware reads or writes configuration registers, commonly I2C or SPI on an audio codec. Required startup programming depends on the exact chip, reset defaults and hardware mode.
A variant of the I2S-style audio format in which each word's MSB starts exactly on the word-clock edge, one bit clock earlier than in standard I2S. Mixing up the two misreads every sample by one bit.
example: The Daisy Seed Rev 7 runs its PCM3060 in 24-bit left-justified format.

definition: A variant of the I2S-style format in which each word ends exactly at the next word-clock edge, so its position depends on the word length.
Time-division multiplexing: sending several channels on one data line by giving each a time slot in turn. Audio TDM extends I2S to more than two channels.
Serial audio interface: the STM32 peripheral that sends and receives I2S-style audio, generating the clocks and working with DMA. SAI1 is its first instance.
Left/right clock (also word select or frame sync): the I2S signal that marks which channel's word is being sent. It completes one cycle per frame, so it runs at the sample rate.
example: In a standard two-channel I2S frame at 48 kHz, one LRCLK cycle carries the left and right words.

definition: Master clock: a fast clock, a fixed multiple of the sample rate such as 256 times, that many codecs need to run their converters and filters.
example: 256 × 44.1 kHz is about 11.29 MHz.

definition: Serial clock: the clock line of a synchronous serial bus. On SPI it is the bus clock; in I2S tables it is another name for the bit clock (BCLK).
An abbreviation with two meanings here: Secure Digital, the memory-card format (SD card); and, in I2S signal tables, serial data, the line that carries the sample bits.
An abbreviation with two meanings here: the round DIN connector (after the German standards body) used for MIDI ports; and, on codec pin labels, data in. DOUT is the matching data out.
Data out: a pin label for a chip's serial data output, for example a codec's ADC data going to the microcontroller.
One sample for every channel at a single instant: for stereo, a left and a right sample. In I2S, one word-clock cycle carries one frame.
example: At 48 kHz there are 48,000 stereo frames a second.

definition: The fixed-length part of a frame reserved for one channel's word. A 16-bit sample may sit in a 32-bit slot with the rest left as padding.
A signal that swings both above and below zero, as audio does, rather than staying in a positive range such as 0 to 1.

Direct memory access: a hardware unit that copies data between memory and peripherals without the CPU. For audio it streams samples between a RAM buffer and the I2S/SAI peripheral, interrupting the CPU only when a block is done.
example: With DMA, the CPU is interrupted once per 48-sample block instead of 48,000 times a second.

definition: Using two buffers (or two halves of one) so one can be used, for example played by DMA, while the other is filled. They swap roles each block.
example: libDaisy's DMA buffer is two halves, each holding one block for two channels.

definition: The DMA interrupt raised when a circular transfer reaches the middle of its buffer; the 'complete' interrupt is raised at the end. Each tells the CPU one half is free to refill.
A fixed-size array used as a queue whose read and write positions wrap round from the end to the start. It needs no allocation after start-up, which suits real-time audio.
The analogue circuit after a DAC that conditions the signal for the outside world, for example with a coupling capacitor, an op-amp buffer, filtering or a headphone amplifier.

A series capacitor used with the surrounding impedances to pass changing signal components while rejecting steady DC transfer after settling. Its stored voltage can be nonzero; its capacitance and load set a high-pass response.
Connecting a signal through a capacitor so only its changing (AC) part passes and any DC offset is blocked.
example: The Daisy Seed's audio inputs are AC coupled.

definition: Direct current: current with one direction, though its magnitude can vary. In audio discussion, a DC component means the constant or mean signal offset; a coupling capacitor rejects steady transfer after settling.
Alternating current: current that repeatedly changes direction. In audio discussion AC also refers to a changing voltage component; actual equipment signals can include a DC offset.
Operational amplifier: a versatile amplifier chip used for buffers, gain stages and active filters. An op-amp buffer lets a weak source drive a cable or load.
A small amplifier that can drive headphones' low impedance (tens of ohms), which a line output cannot do well.

An input with gain suited to small microphone signals. A line-level source may overload it unless the specific interface offers a suitable pad or line mode; check its manual and disable inappropriate phantom power.
An audio-interface input designed for guitars and similar sources, with a high input impedance and adjustable gain.

DC power supplied through microphone signal conductors, commonly 48 V on balanced microphone connections. It can power compatible microphones or other designed equipment; disable it when connecting an incompatible line source and follow the equipment manuals.
A microphone that senses sound with a charged capacitor and needs power, often phantom power.
Recording an output straight back into an input so the total delay of the path can be measured from the recording.
Listening to a signal as it is played or recorded. Monitoring through a DAW adds that program's buffer to the latency.

The negative slope of a filter’s phase response with angular frequency, expressing frequency-dependent envelope delay. Constant group delay within a band aligns those components in time; magnitude filtering can still alter waveform shape.
example: The PCM3060 datasheet specifies DAC digital-filter group delay as 20 sample periods.

definition: Sending data one bit at a time over a single line (per direction), as UART, I2C, SPI and I2S all do, rather than many bits at once on parallel wires.
example: Teensy 4.1 has eight hardware serial ports.

definition: A shared serial connection that several devices can use, such as I2C or SPI.
Serial communication with a separate clock line, so the receiver knows exactly when to read each bit. I2C, SPI and I2S are synchronous.
Serial communication with no clock wire: both ends agree a bit rate in advance and the receiver times bits from a start bit. UARTs, and so MIDI, work this way.

Universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter: a peripheral that sends and receives bytes as asynchronous serial on one wire each way (TX and RX). A USART can also run synchronously. DIN MIDI is a UART link.
example: MIDI runs a UART at 31,250 baud, 8-N-1.

definition: Transmit (TX) and receive (RX): the two data lines of a UART. One device's TX connects to the other's RX.
The number of signal symbols sent per second; for a UART each symbol is one bit, so it is the bit rate. Both ends must use the same rate.
example: MIDI's 31,250 baud gives 32 µs per bit.

definition: The 0 bit that begins every UART frame, pulling the idle-high line low. The receiver times the following bits from its falling edge.
The 1 bit that ends every UART frame, returning the line to idle. If the receiver finds a 0 there, it reports a framing error.
An optional extra bit in a serial frame used to detect single-bit errors. MIDI does not use one.
A UART framing setting with eight data bits, no parity and one stop bit. Including the start bit, a byte occupies ten bit times on the wire.
A UART error reported when the stop bit is not where it should be, usually because the two ends' baud rates differ or the line was disturbed.

Inter-Integrated Circuit: a two-wire synchronous bus (SCL clock and SDA data) on which a controller talks to many devices, each with its own address. It is slow but simple, and is used to configure codecs, sensors and small displays.
example: Fast-mode I2C runs at 400 kHz.

definition: Serial data: the bidirectional data line of an I2C bus.
Serial clock: the I2C bus clock, driven by the controller.
The number, usually 7 bits, that identifies a device on an I2C bus. The controller sends it first in every transaction, and only the device with that address replies.
example: A 7-bit address allows 128 values, of which 16 are reserved.

definition: Acknowledge: the receiver pulls SDA low during the ninth I2C clock to indicate acceptance. During a read the controller deliberately leaves this slot high (NACK) after its final requested data byte.

Not acknowledge: SDA remains high in an I2C ninth-clock slot. On an ordinary target-address attempt no target acknowledged; wrong address, wiring, power or a busy target are possible causes. A controller deliberately NACKs its final received byte.
The I2C signal that begins a transaction: SDA falls while SCL is high. It is a bus condition, not a data bit.
The I2C signal that ends a transaction: SDA rises while SCL is high.
An output that can only pull a line low or let go, never drive it high. A pull-up resistor supplies the high level, so several devices can share a line without fighting. I2C uses it.

An output stage with two devices: one pushes (drives the output high or positive) and the other pulls (drives it low or negative). A push-pull digital output therefore drives a line actively both ways, giving faster edges than open-drain, which is one reason SPI is faster than I2C; push-pull audio amplifiers use the same idea.
The total capacitance of a bus's wires and connected devices. With the pull-up resistance it sets how fast an open-drain line can rise, limiting I2C speed and length.
An I2C feature that lets a slow device hold SCL low to pause the controller until it is ready.
The named maximum clock rates of I2C: Standard-mode 100 kbit/s, Fast-mode 400 kbit/s, Fast-mode Plus 1 Mbit/s and High-speed mode 3.4 Mbit/s (plus a write-only Ultra-Fast mode at 5 Mbit/s).

Serial Peripheral Interface: a synchronous bus with a clock, a data line each way and a chip-select line per device. Its push-pull outputs let it run at several to tens of MHz, so it suits displays, flash memory and fast ADCs.
example: Sending a 1,024-byte display frame over 8 MHz SPI takes about 1 ms.

definition: The SPI data line from the controller to the device. COPI (controller out, peripheral in) is the newer name.
The SPI data line from the device back to the controller. CIPO (controller in, peripheral out) is the newer name.

The selection signal used by an SPI peripheral, commonly active low. Independently selected peripherals usually have separate signals; daisy-chained parts and interfaces without selection are documented exceptions.
Clock polarity: the SPI setting for the clock's idle level, 0 for idle low or 1 for idle high.
Clock phase: the SPI setting for which clock edge data is sampled on, 0 for the first edge or 1 for the second.
One of four combinations of CPOL and CPHA (modes 0 to 3) that set how an SPI device expects the clock. Controller and device must agree.
example: Idle high and sampling on the second edge is mode 3.

definition: The SD card's native fast interface, using several data lines, as an alternative to talking to the card over SPI.
A removable flash memory card (Secure Digital). A Raspberry Pi boots from one, which is why it should be shut down cleanly; the Daisy bootloader can load programs from one.
A display made of organic light-emitting diodes, needing no backlight. Small monochrome OLEDs (such as 128 × 64 pixels) are common on synth panels.
example: A 128 × 64 monochrome frame is 1,024 bytes.

definition: A colour LCD driven by thin-film transistors. Its frames are much larger than a monochrome OLED's, so it is usually driven over SPI.
MIDI over the traditional 5-pin DIN connectors: an 8-N-1 UART at 31,250 baud carried as a 5 mA current loop, with an opto-isolator at every MIDI IN.

The receiving MIDI port. Traditional DIN MIDI IN uses the specified opto-isolated circuit so that this data connection does not require the two equipment grounds to be galvanically joined; MIDI OUT is the transmitting port.
MIDI carried over a USB connection instead of DIN cables. It needs one side to be a USB host and can deliver much larger bursts than DIN MIDI.

A MIDI channel message carrying a note number and velocity; nonzero velocity starts a note, while velocity zero means note off. A complete three-byte message takes 960 microseconds on DIN MIDI; running status can omit repeated status bytes.
The MIDI message that ends a note. Losing one leaves a stuck note.

MIDI Control Change. In MIDI 1.0, a channel message carries a controller number and a seven-bit value; paired controls can provide fourteen-bit resolution. MIDI 2.0 Channel Voice Control Change uses a thirty-two-bit value.

A MIDI message-type byte whose most significant bit is one. Channel-message status also contains a channel number; system-message status does not. Running status may omit repeated channel status on the wire.

A MIDI 1.0 channel-message shortcut that can omit repeated channel status bytes. Repeated note messages then need two data bytes after the initial status; System Common messages clear running status, while System Real-Time bytes can interleave without clearing it.
example: Four note-ons with running status take 9 bytes instead of 12.

definition: The MIDI message that asks an instrument to switch preset (program).
One-byte MIDI messages for timing and transport, such as clock, start and stop. They can be sent at any moment, even in the middle of another message.
A note that keeps sounding because its note-off was lost or ignored.
Signalling by switching a current on and off rather than a voltage. DIN MIDI is a 5 mA current loop, which works over longer cables and pairs naturally with an opto-isolator.

A component that transfers a signal using light between electrically isolated input and output circuits. DIN MIDI uses it to isolate its data path; other cables or connections may still join the equipment grounds.
The organisation that publishes and maintains the MIDI specifications.
The MIDI Association's 2014 update to the MIDI 1.0 electrical specification, which gives the current-loop circuit, including resistor values for 3.3 V and 5 V transmitters.
A button you tap in time with the music so the device measures and sets its tempo.

A hardware or software request handled through a processor exception/interrupt mechanism. Eligible enabled requests can preempt lower-priority work; masking, priorities and processor state determine when a handler actually executes.
The function the CPU runs when an interrupt fires. It should be short and must never wait, because it blocks other work at its priority and below.
A number that decides which interrupt runs when several are pending, and whether one may interrupt another. On Arm Cortex-M a lower number means higher priority.
example: The Teensy Audio Library runs its DSP from a software interrupt at priority 208, where 255 is the lowest.

definition: Suspending current execution so higher-priority eligible work can run, then resuming it. Enabled, unmasked interrupts can preempt a bare-metal main loop; priority and masking determine which handlers can preempt each other.
An interrupt triggered by code setting it pending rather than by hardware. The Teensy Audio Library's DMA interrupt pends one so the long audio update runs at a lower priority.
An interrupt that fires when a GPIO input changes level. Wiring a bouncy switch to one fires it many times per press, so switches are better polled.
The endless loop firmware runs after setup, whenever no interrupt is active. Knob scanning, MIDI parsing, displays and logging belong here, not in the audio callback.
In firmware, the main loop and other low-priority work, as opposed to the interrupt-driven audio callback (sometimes called the background).
A function you hand to a library so the library can call it later when something happens, such as 'a block of audio is needed'.

In audio code, the number of samples per channel processed in each audio callback. It sets the processing budget (block size divided by sample rate) and adds to latency. (Storage and ciphers use 'block size' for a different idea: the fixed chunk of bytes they work in.)
example: libDaisy defaults to 48 samples at 48 kHz; the Teensy Audio Library to 128 at 44.1 kHz.

definition: The time one audio block lasts: block size divided by sample rate. It is the deadline for the callback.
example: 128 samples at 44.1 kHz last about 2.9 ms.

definition: The latest time by which the required audio work must finish before hardware reuses its buffer. A missed deadline may produce stale/partial samples, a dropout or another data-dependent audible fault.

A system whose correctness includes meeting specified time constraints. Audio work must deliver the needed samples by its deadline; missing it risks stale or incomplete data and an audible fault, whose form depends on the signal and buffering.

Timing with known, repeatable limits under specified assumptions. Bare-metal firmware makes some scheduling factors explicit, but interrupt interference, memory behavior and work bounds still need analysis; an OS can also provide real-time scheduling facilities.

Execution whose worst-case duration is limited under explicit platform and input assumptions. Audio work needs sufficient timing margin; observed maxima from a finite benchmark alone do not establish a universal worst-case bound.

The total delay from an action to its visible or audible result, counting every stage in between rather than just one. For a synth, from pressing a key to hearing the sound, it adds MIDI transmission, waiting for a block, buffering and converter delay, then the audio interface and DAW.
example: A simplified 48-sample, 48 kHz model gives about 3.4 ms including a full three-byte DIN message, next-block adoption, one output block and the assumed DAC delay. It excludes extra parsing, interface and host buffering.

definition: Audio callback work exceeding the available deadline interval. Hardware may then consume stale or partly updated samples; actual audible effects depend on data and buffering.
example: A callback taking 3.1 ms of a 2.9 ms budget overruns.

definition: The fraction of the processor's available time that is being used. For audio code it is the callback's run time divided by the block period: above 100% blocks are late, and the maximum matters more than the average.
example: 300,000 of 480,000 available cycles is 62.5% load.

definition: A hardware counter that counts CPU clock cycles, used to time code precisely. On Cortex-M3/M4/M7 it is the DWT's CYCCNT register: optional, and off until firmware enables it.
example: At 600 MHz the 32-bit counter wraps about every 7 seconds.

definition: Data Watchpoint and Trace: a Cortex-M debug unit that provides watchpoints and the CYCCNT cycle counter.
libDaisy's class for measuring the audio callback's average, minimum and maximum load: call OnBlockStart and OnBlockEnd in the callback and read the results from the main loop.
A Teensy Audio Library function that returns the highest percentage of CPU any audio update has used, which PJRC calls the most useful check that processing is within limits.
Teensy Audio Library functions that briefly hold off the audio update (AudioNoInterrupts) and release it (AudioInterrupts), so a group of settings takes effect at the same time.

libDaisy's control class that normalises an ADC value and applies a one-state smoother. Its checked source defaults the slew setting to 0.002 s and uses a coefficient rule different from the lesson's exponential time-constant rule; rate and configuration matter.

Requesting memory at runtime, for example with malloc or new. General-purpose allocators do not usually provide the bounded, nonblocking timing contract needed by an audio callback and may fail or take locks; preallocate the required callback storage.
When free memory is split into many small gaps, so a large request can fail even though enough memory is free in total. A long-running instrument that allocates is at risk.
Reserving all the memory a program needs at start-up (voice pools, delay buffers, queues) so nothing is allocated while audio runs.
The C function that formats text and writes it out. In an audio callback it is unsafe: formatting takes variable time and the output may block when its buffer is full.
Recording what a program is doing as text messages. In real-time code, log from the main loop and have the callback only set flags or counters.
A text connection (over USB or a UART) that firmware prints debug messages to and a computer displays.
When a high-priority task is stuck waiting for a lock held by a low-priority task, which itself may not get to run, so the urgent task waits far longer than its deadline.
A mechanism that lets only one piece of code use a shared resource at a time; others must wait. Waiting is forbidden in the audio callback, so real-time code uses lock-free techniques.

A concurrency progress property: system-wide progress does not depend on acquiring a lock. It does not guarantee a fixed completion time for every operation or thread; an audio callback needs an appropriate bounded implementation, such as verified SPSC loads/stores.
example: A single-producer/single-consumer ring buffer is lock-free.

definition: An operation that happens as one indivisible step, so no other code can see it half-done. Atomic types in C++ also provide memory-ordering guarantees.
example: Verify the exact atomic type and operation on the selected compiler/target; neither width nor the absence of an OS automatically proves lock-free or bounded execution.

definition: An atomic read-modify-write that adds to a variable and returns the old value in one indivisible step, so no update is lost.

Arm instructions that mark an exclusive access and then conditionally attempt a store. The store can fail if the exclusive monitor was cleared, including by intervening writes or exception behavior; read-modify-write implementations may need retries. Armv7-M has byte, halfword and word forms, without a 64-bit exclusive pair.
The rules for when one thread's or interrupt's writes become visible to another, and in what order. Without explicit ordering, compilers and CPUs may reorder memory accesses.

A memory-ordering pairing: a release store makes all earlier writes visible before it, and an acquire load that sees that store also sees those writes. It is how one side safely publishes data to the other.
example: The ring-buffer producer writes the item, then release-stores head; the consumer acquire-loads head, then reads the item.

definition: The weakest atomic memory ordering: the operation itself is indivisible, but it orders no other memory accesses. It is enough for a lone value nothing else depends on.

A compiler or processor ordering mechanism that constrains specified memory accesses. The exact ordering and visibility depend on the architecture and barrier; correctly chosen atomics express the required language-level synchronization.
The compiler or processor performing memory reads and writes in a different order from the source code, which is invisible to a single thread but can break communication between two.

A C and C++ keyword telling the compiler that every access to a variable must really happen, because hardware may change it. It is right for hardware registers but is not thread or interrupt synchronisation.
Reading a value that takes more than one memory operation while another side is halfway through writing it, so you get half old and half new data.
example: A 64-bit value on a 32-bit core can tear.

definition: An out-of-date copy of a variable, for example one the compiler kept in a register so a loop never sees another side's update.
When two sides read-modify-write the same variable and one side's write overwrites the other's, so a change disappears.

An operation that obtains a value, computes a replacement and stores it. A plain increment can lose concurrent updates; a language atomic read-modify-write supplies indivisibility, while its implementation and progress still depend on the target.
A compiler optimisation that moves an operation out of a loop because it seems not to change, such as reading a variable once instead of every pass.
Single-producer/single-consumer: a queue with exactly one writer (the producer) and one reader (the consumer). Each index has one writer, so it can be built lock-free with atomic loads and stores.
example: A MIDI parser in the main loop pushing note events to the audio callback is an SPSC arrangement.

definition: First in, first out: items leave a queue in the order they arrived.

A queue carrying discrete events such as note transitions. Accepted items can be delivered in order; finite capacity and consumption limits mean overflow requires an explicit detection and recovery policy.

An integer type representing non-negative values. Fixed-width unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo its range; elapsed-counter subtraction is valid only with the intended width and a known interval below one wrap.
A C or C++ type grouping several named fields into one value, such as a preset's parameters.
Electro-Smith's audio microcontroller board: an STM32H750 Cortex-M7 at 480 MHz, 64 MB SDRAM, 8 MB flash and a stereo audio codec, programmed in C++ with libDaisy.
example: The Rev 7 Seed uses a PCM3060 codec and outputs 1 V RMS at full scale.

definition: The company that makes the Daisy audio platform and its libDaisy and DaisySP libraries.
Electro-Smith's C++ hardware library for Daisy boards: it sets up the codec and DMA, calls your audio callback with float samples, and provides classes for knobs, switches and CPU-load measurement.
Electro-Smith's C++ library of DSP building blocks such as oscillators, filters and envelopes.
A family of small microcontroller development boards from PJRC. The Teensy 4.1 has an NXP i.MX RT1062 Cortex-M7 at 600 MHz, 1,024 KB RAM and 8 MB flash, and is programmed through the Arduino IDE.
The organisation behind the Teensy hardware design and software, including the Teensy Audio Library and audio adaptor. Check the product page for current manufacturing and distribution details.
A US electronics company that sells hobbyist boards. PJRC's Teensy 4.1 page states that SparkFun is now manufacturing Teensy products.
PJRC's add-on board for Teensy with an SGTL5000 codec (16-bit, 44.1 kHz), headphone and line outputs, and line or mic input, controlled over I2C.
PJRC's C++ audio toolkit for Teensy. Audio objects process 128-sample blocks of 16-bit integers at 44.1 kHz, updated from a low-priority software interrupt.
NXP's Cortex-M7 'crossover' microcontroller used on Teensy 4.x, running at 600 MHz. It has no internal flash, so programs live in an external flash chip.
STMicroelectronics' family of Arm Cortex-M microcontrollers. The STM32H750 on the Daisy Seed has a Cortex-M7 at up to 480 MHz and 128 KB of internal flash.
A European chip maker (often shortened to ST) that makes the STM32 microcontrollers and ST-Link debug probes.
A family of small, low-cost Linux computers. The Raspberry Pi 5 has a quad-core Cortex-A76 at 2.4 GHz and a 40-pin GPIO header but no analogue audio output or ADC.
A complete computer on one circuit board, such as a Raspberry Pi, typically running a full operating system like Linux.
Hardware Attached on Top: an add-on board that plugs onto a Raspberry Pi's GPIO header and identifies itself through an EEPROM. Audio HATs add DACs or codecs.
Raspberry Pi's audio HAT built around a TI PCM5122 DAC: 24-bit 192 kHz line out (0–2 V RMS on phono sockets) and a headphone amplifier, with no inputs.
Raspberry Pi's range of audio HATs: the DAC+ and DAC Pro (output only) and the Codec Zero, which adds inputs.
A free, open-source operating system kernel, used with other software as the OS on Raspberry Pi computers. Audio on it runs through ALSA with OS buffering.
Advanced Linux Sound Architecture: Linux's built-in audio layer, which provides the drivers and buffering between programs and sound hardware.
A small file that tells the Linux kernel what extra hardware is attached, such as a HAT that cannot identify itself automatically.
Universal Serial Bus: the standard connection for power and data between computers and devices. Every link has one host, usually a computer, and one or more devices.
The side of a USB link that controls the bus, usually a computer. Two USB devices cannot talk to each other without a host.
example: Teensy 4.1 has a host interface; a supported host stack, suitable cable, power budget and compatible USB MIDI device are still required.

definition: The side of a USB link that responds to the host, such as a keyboard or audio interface.
USB On-The-Go: a feature that lets a port act as either host or device.

A standardised USB behavior for a device category, such as audio, MIDI or DFU. A matching OS class driver can avoid a vendor-specific driver, but class version, OS support and required features still determine compatibility.
A reversible USB connector that can also carry higher power.
example: The Raspberry Pi 5 takes 5 V at up to 5 A over USB-C.

definition: A small, older USB connector, used on the Daisy Seed.
A round coaxial audio connector (RCA), common on consumer audio gear.
The small round audio connector used for headphones and consumer line signals. The Raspberry Pi 5 has none.
Elektron's drum machine and sampler with MIDI and USB, part of the user's studio and a candidate controller for the synth.
Cycling '74's visual programming environment for audio; its Gen~ extension can generate code for platforms such as Daisy.
A lossy compressed audio file format. Its software encoders and decoders are also called codecs, which is a different meaning from a hardware audio codec.
Digital signal processing: computing on sampled signals, such as generating, filtering and mixing audio. It is the work the audio callback does.

Personal computer: a general-purpose computer intended for individual use. Traditional serial interfaces expose selected standard baud rates, but support for a particular rate depends on the interface and driver.

A table that scores each option on several criteria, multiplies each score by a weight for how much that criterion matters, and adds them up. It makes priorities explicit but is only as good as its weights.
A pass/fail requirement applied before scoring: an option that fails one is out, however well it scores elsewhere.
Checking how much a result changes when its assumptions, such as weights, change. If a small, defensible change flips the winner, the options are effectively tied.
A short document recording a decision, the options, the evidence and the reasons, so it can be understood and revisited later.
The complete list of parts needed to build something, with quantities.

A data structure where items are added at one end and removed from the other in arrival order (first in, first out). In firmware, queues carry events such as notes from the main loop to the audio callback.

A controlled transition of a parameter through intermediate values over a chosen sample duration. A linear parameter ramp uses equal increments; it may span blocks, and endpoint conventions and floating-point rounding depend on the implementation. Smoothing can reduce clicks or zipper noise but does not guarantee inaudibility.
example: A nominal 480 Hz cutoff change over 48 increments uses 10 Hz per increment, with explicit endpoint handling.

definition: Uniform Resource Locator: a web address. Recording the URL and date of each product fact lets you re-check it later.

A source of electrical power at specified voltage/current limits for a circuit, such as a documented low-voltage USB supply. Supply variations can couple into ADC readings and audio, depending on the circuit and filtering.
Sending the least significant bit (the bit worth the least) of each byte first on a serial line. UARTs, and so MIDI, send data LSB first, the opposite of I2S's MSB-first audio words.
example: The byte 0x01 sent LSB first puts its single 1 bit straight after the start bit.

definition: A startup interval during which a bootloader looks for an update or programming request before launching application firmware. The fetched Daisy bootloader guide documents 2.5 seconds; this is not an OS shutdown interval.

Work paid once per audio invocation, such as interrupt entry, buffer bookkeeping and function dispatch. Smaller blocks pay it more times per second, leaving a smaller fraction of the budget for sample processing.

term: CPU clock cycles per audio frame
aliases: CPU clock cycles per audio frame
definition: Processor clock ticks consumed or available while computing one sample for every audio channel. These are CPU cycles, not oscillator waveform cycles; memory and interrupts also consume time.
The physical case holding the synth electronics, controls, connectors and display. It needs appropriate mechanical fit and protection; it is a different concept from a tuned loudspeaker enclosure.
A proportion expressed in hundredths. A CPU-load measurement of 60 percent uses sixty hundredths of the stated block budget.

A bus exchange beginning with START, followed by addressing and data clocked with acknowledgement slots, and ending with STOP or continuing through a repeated START. The controller and addressed target follow the I2C protocol; this is a different meaning from a database transaction.

Memory that stores a sequence of sample values for processing or transfer. Its capacity, channel layout, current contents and ownership matter; the buffer is storage, while buffer size is the count of values it holds.
example: In the described stereo double-buffered DMA output, each released half stores one block that the CPU refills before DMA reuses it.

definition: The side of a serial audio link that generates the bit clock and frame/word clock. The other side follows those clocks; the codec or MCU role must match the selected hardware configuration.

The side of a serial audio link that accepts the bit and word/frame clocks from another device. Manufacturer documentation commonly calls this slave mode; it must be configured to match the generating device and sample format.

A version number identifying one complete published parameter set. The producer and consumer use it with the buffer index and an acknowledgement to coordinate ownership; the combined representation must use suitable target-supported atomic operations.
The MIDI port that transmits messages to another device. A traditional DIN MIDI OUT drives the specified current-loop circuit; the destination MIDI IN provides the receiving opto-isolated circuit.
